messages:
Elliot Price: Trying to lock customer-facing wording for Optimize Guardrails docs (PR up in redwood-docs/pr_322). Main issue: what do we call a “quality regression” and how do we explain a blocked apply without implying Redwood “broke” the model?

Elliot Price: Draft copy currently says: “Apply blocked due to quality regression.” Feels too loaded. Looking for alignment w/ Product + ML + Support.

Kenji Nakamura: +1 “regression” reads like we shipped something bad. For UI and docs, we’ve been leaning on “did not meet guardrail thresholds” / “quality checks failed”.

Kenji Nakamura: Maybe reserve “regression” for internal / post-change monitoring, not for gating outcome.

Wei Chen: Agree. “Regression” is technically correct (delta vs baseline), but customer doesn’t care about baseline mechanics.

Wei Chen: Suggest: “The proposed optimization did not meet your configured quality thresholds on the evaluation suite.” Then a link “What is an evaluation suite?”

Aditya Rao: From PM perspective: we should be explicit that we ran evals and blocked to protect them. Something like:
- “Blocked to prevent potential quality degradation”
- Provide the top failing metrics + confidence
But avoid blaming the customer prompts or implying their app is wrong.

Selene Huang: +1 to “did not meet thresholds”. Also we need to be careful with “potential”. In gating we are making a decision based on measured deltas.

Selene Huang: Recommended phrasing (ML side):
- “This change failed guardrail checks”
- “One or more quality metrics fell below the allowed threshold compared to baseline.”
Then in expanded section explain baseline = current deployed config for that route/model.

Owen Phillips: From Support: the word “regression” triggers escalation 100%. We get “your platform regressed our model” tickets.

Owen Phillips: What works in tickets is: “Optimize attempted to apply a cost optimization, but Guardrails blocked it because the evaluation results didn’t meet the required quality bar.” Then: “No production traffic was changed.” That last sentence is key.

Naomi Feldman: Also watch absolutes. If we say “quality degraded” that can be read as “we know your outputs are worse” even if eval suite is proxy.

Naomi Feldman: Safer: “did not meet threshold” + “based on the configured evaluation suite” + “you can review the results and rerun or request an override (if enabled)”.

Kira Thompson: For runbooks we use “hard-block” and “soft-block” (override). For public docs, I’d avoid “hard/soft” and instead say:
- “Blocked”
- “Blocked—override required”
And explain who can override + audit logging.

Elliot Price: Super helpful. So for docs headline: “Apply blocked” not “quality regression”.

Elliot Price: Proposed updated phrasing:
1) Short: “Blocked: Guardrails checks did not meet the required quality thresholds.”
2) Add reassurance line: “Your serving configuration was not changed.”
3) Explain next steps: “View results, adjust prompt set/suite, rerun, or request override (enterprise/admin).”

Kenji Nakamura: That matches UI direction. Also for the “failed” state, we want to show a summary like:
- Metric: task_success
- Baseline: 0.84
- Proposed: 0.79
- Threshold: max drop 0.02
But docs can keep it conceptual.

Wei Chen: +1. And please avoid “we detected a quality issue” language. It implies runtime bug.

Selene Huang: One nuance: it’s not always relative drop; some metrics are absolute floors (e.g., toxicity ceiling). So docs should say “thresholds” not “regression vs baseline” everywhere.

Selene Huang: Maybe a line: “Guardrails evaluate multiple quality metrics (e.g., task success, formatting compliance, safety) and compare results against thresholds.”

Aditya Rao: Also include a note that different optimization types can require different suites. Folks get confused why quantization requires more checks than caching.

Owen Phillips: +1 and please add a short callout for “Timeout” state. We’ve had confusion already (“did it apply or not??”). The message needs to be unambiguous: “Not applied.”

Elliot Price: Good catch. We should align language for timeout too.

Kira Thompson: Suggest timeout copy:
- “Unable to complete guardrail evaluation in time. The change was not applied.”
- “Try again or contact support if this persists.”
And if customer tier allows manual approval, mention “request override”.

Naomi Feldman: +1. Also for override: we need to say “with audit logging” (customers ask for this explicitly). But don’t overshare internal controls.

Naomi Feldman: Simple line: “If your org allows overrides, an authorized admin can approve applying the change with a justification recorded in audit logs.”

Kenji Nakamura: Small wording tweak: “authorized member” vs “admin” (RBAC can be custom). Maybe “authorized role”.

Elliot Price: OK. Here’s the final set I’ll apply to docs + sync w/ UI strings:

Elliot Price: **Blocked**: “Guardrails checks did not meet the required quality thresholds for this change. Your serving configuration was not changed.”

Elliot Price: **Blocked — override required**: “Guardrails checks did not meet the required quality thresholds. This change requires an override from an authorized role and will be recorded in audit logs.”

Elliot Price: **Timeout**: “Guardrails evaluation did not complete in time. This change was not applied. You can retry or contact support if timeouts continue.”

Selene Huang: Works for me. Minor: for timeout, don’t promise “contact support” as solution, but it’s fine.

Aditya Rao: +1. Please add “View evaluation results” link in docs flow. That’s the top CTA.

Wei Chen: +1. I’ll add a short section describing “evaluation suite”, “prompt set revision”, and “baseline = current config” so it’s less magical.

Owen Phillips: Thanks. The “was not changed / was not applied” line will save us a ton of back-and-forth.

Naomi Feldman: Looks good. If you mention audit logs, please also mention retention is per plan (or just say “available in audit logs” without specifics).

Elliot Price: Will do. I’ll push an update to PR_322 today + ask Kenji to sanity check UI parity. :thumbsup:

Kenji Nakamura: 👍 will review once it’s up.

Selene Huang: 👍

Owen Phillips: 🙌
